prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I teach my friend, a fisherman gone blind, to cast true left, right or center and how far between lily pads and the fallen cedar. Darkness is precious, how long will darkness last? Our bait, worms, have no professors, they live in darkness, can be taught fear of light. Cut into threes even sixes they live separate lives, recoil from light. He tells me, “I am seldom blind when I dream, morning is anthracite, I play blind man’s bluff, I cannot find myself, my shoe, the sink, tell time, but that’s spilled milk and ink, the lost and found I cannot find. I can tell the difference between a mollusk and a whelk, a grieving liar and a lemon rind.” Laughing, he says, “I still hope the worm will turn,pink, lank, and warm, dined out on apples of good fortune. Books have a faintly legible smell. Divorced from the sun, I am a kind of bachelor henpecked by the night. Sometimes I use my darkness well— in the overcast and sunlight of my mind. I can still wink, sing, my eyes are songs.” Darkness is precious, how long will darkness last? He could not fish, he could not walk, he fell in his own feces. He wept. He died where he fell.The power of beauty to right all wrongs is hard for me to sell.

outputs.L1:
I teach my friend—a fisherman gone blind—to cast true, left, right, or center, and to judge how far to reach between the lily pads and the fallen cedar. Darkness is precious; how long will darkness last? Our bait, the worms, have no professors, yet they dwell in darkness and can be taught to fear the light. Cut into threes, even sixes, they live their separate lives, recoiling from the light.

He tells me, "I am seldom blind when I dream. Morning is anthracite, and I play blind man's bluff—I cannot find myself, my shoe, the sink, nor tell the time; but that is spilled milk and ink, the lost and found I cannot find. Still, I can tell the difference between a mollusk and a whelk, between a grieving liar and a lemon rind."

Laughing, he says, "I still hope the worm will turn—pink, lank, and warm—having dined out on the apples of good fortune. Books carry a faintly legible smell. Divorced from the sun, I am a kind of bachelor, henpecked by the night. Sometimes I use my darkness well, amid the overcast and sunlight of my mind. I can still wink, still sing; my eyes are songs."

Darkness is precious; how long will darkness last? He could not fish, he could not walk; he fell in his own filth. He wept. He died where he fell. The power of beauty to right all wrongs is a truth I find hard to sell.
outputs.L2:
I'm teaching a friend of mine—a fisherman who lost his sight—how to make his line land accurately to the left, the right, or straight ahead, and how to gauge the distance across the water separating the lily pads from the toppled cedar. How valuable the dark is; I wonder how long it will hold. The worms we use as bait have never studied under any teacher, yet they dwell in shadow and can learn to dread the light. Slice them into three pieces, or even six, and each fragment carries on its own existence, shrinking away from brightness.

He confides to me, "When I'm dreaming, my blindness rarely troubles me. The dawn arrives black as coal, and I stumble through it like a game of blind man's bluff—unable to locate my own body, my shoe, the basin, or read the hour. But those are trivial losses, like milk knocked over or spilled ink; the lost and found is one thing I'll never track down. Still, I know a mollusk from a whelk, and I can distinguish a mourning liar from a twist of lemon peel."

With a laugh, he adds, "I keep hoping the worm might change—turning pink, stretched thin, and warm, feasting on the fruits of lucky chances. Old books give off a scent you can barely make out. Cut off from daylight, I've become a sort of unmarried man nagged and ruled by the night. Now and then I put my darkness to good purpose—amid the clouds and brightness within my thoughts. I can wink and sing yet; my very eyes are melodies."

How valuable the dark is; I wonder how long it will hold. In the end, fishing was beyond him, and so was walking. He collapsed into his own waste. He shed tears. And in the very spot where he fell, he died. Convincing others—or myself—that beauty has the strength to mend every injustice is something I struggle to do.
outputs.L3:
# Teaching in Darkness

I taught my blind friend how to fish, guiding his hands until he learned to cast his line with an accuracy that seemed impossible for a man who had never seen the water's surface. Together we baited our hooks with worms—those small, living things that writhed and recoiled against our fingers, twisting in a darkness not unlike the one my friend inhabited every waking hour. He handled them without flinching, understanding their blind panic better than I ever could.

Sometimes he would speak of his dreams, and how strange it was that he could see clearly there—colors, faces, the sharp edges of a world that eluded him by day. It was the ordinary tasks that defeated him: fumbling for a lost shoe in the morning, or running his fingers hopelessly across the face of a clock, unable to read the hour. In sleep he was whole; awake, he stumbled through a fog of small confusions.

Yet his blindness had never dulled his other gifts. His remaining senses had grown keen and precise, able to distinguish subtle differences that I, with all my sight, would overlook—the change in a bird's song, the shift in the wind, the particular weight of silence before rain. His wit stayed sharp as ever. He had found, in his own way, how to use his darkness well, turning what should have been only loss into a strange and quiet mastery.

He never surrendered his hope or his humor. "I can still wink," he would insist, closing one useless eye with a grin, "and I can still sing." He called his eyes his "songs," as though the light they could not gather had simply moved inward, becoming music instead. In this he seemed almost content, a man who had made peace with his affliction by refusing to let it silence him.

But the story does not end in peace. In time my friend began to fail, his body weakening until one day he fell and did not rise again—he died there, in the place where he had fallen, alone with his inner songs. And I am left to wonder whether all the beauty he found, all the sweetness he wrung from his darkness, could ever truly right so deep a wrong. I doubt it can. Some griefs are not redeemed by grace; they simply remain.
outputs.L4:
# Casting Lines in Darkness

I taught him how to hold the rod, my hands
wrapped over his, the way you'd guide a child—
though he was older, weathered, and his eyes
held nothing but a milky, distant white.

"You feel the water breathing," I would say,
"before you feel the fish." And he would smile,
tilt back his head to catch the morning sun
he could not see but claimed to still recall.

We fished the shallows where the current slowed.
I named the colors of the passing world:
the copper reeds, the green-black of the pines,
the silver flashing when a trout broke free.

He'd listen, nod, and answer with his own
philosophy of shadow. "You believe
that sight is everything," he told me once,
"but I have learned to see another way.

My dreams are stranger now—they have no walls,
no faces I must recognize, no light
to tell me where the edges of things end.
I drift through them like water through my hands.

There is a strength that lives inside the dark.
When everything is taken, what remains
is stubborn, small, and hard as a river stone.
I hold to that. It is my only lamp."

And I believed him. God, I wanted to.
I thought his blindness was a kind of grace,
a deeper vision granted to the few
who suffer beautifully and don't complain.

I thought there was a lesson in his calm,
a poem I could carry home and keep,
some proof that beauty answers every wound,
that art can stitch the torn world back to whole.

But that was my invention, not his life.

The winter took him slowly, piece by piece.
His hands forgot the motion of the cast.
His mind unraveled like a fraying line.
The strength he spoke of thinned to almost nothing.

I found him in the end, alone, undone,
fouled in his own filth upon the floor,
no dignity, no wisdom in his eyes—
just terror and the animal of need.

He did not die into some quiet light.
He did not teach me anything but this:
that suffering is suffering, and no verse,
no perfect line, no image I can shape

will lift him from that room or clean his skin
or give the darkness back its borrowed meaning.
I used to think the power of beauty could
right all the wrongs. I cannot think it now.

I hold the rod. The water still breathes on.
The trout still flash their silver in the sun.
And none of it—not one bright thing—can reach
the place where he lies broken, past my words.
outputs.L5:
# Finding Light in the Cut

There are moments when **darkness** settles over everything we know, wrapping around **our** hopes like a heavy fog. It can feel absolute, as though no light could ever break through.

Yet even the deepest night eventually gives way. A single **cut** in the veil—a thin line of dawn—is all it takes to remind us that morning always comes.

## When Darkness Falls

**Darkness** is more than the absence of light. It is the weight of uncertainty, the quiet that follows loss, and the fear of not knowing what lies ahead. We have all felt it at one time or another, sitting with us in silent rooms and sleepless hours.

But **darkness** also has a purpose. It teaches us patience. It shows us how brightly even the smallest spark can shine when everything around it has gone dim.

## Our Shared Journey

None of us walks alone. **Our** struggles, though deeply personal, echo the struggles of others who have stood where we stand. **Our** stories connect us, thread by thread, into something larger than ourselves.

When we share **our** burdens, they grow lighter. When we lend **our** strength to another, we discover we had more to give than we ever imagined.

## The First Cut of Dawn

The word **cut** carries many meanings. A **cut** can wound, but it can also open a path. When the horizon splits and the first light **cuts** through the sky, it signals that the long night is ending.

Sometimes we must make our own **cut**—a decisive break from what holds us back, a clean line between the past and the future we are building.

---

So when **darkness** surrounds you, remember: **our** shared hope is strong, and a single **cut** of light is enough to begin again.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem about teaching a blind fisherman friend, exploring darkness, worms as bait, and the limits of beauty to redeem suffering.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Water Knows

You asked me once to describe the sunrise, and I failed you. Not because there were no words, but because every word I owned was made of light—*golden, radiant, luminous*—coins from a country you'd never visit. So I put a worm in your hand instead.

Here, I said. This is what I know how to teach.

Your fingers learned the worm the way they learn everything: completely. The cold coil of it, the muscular protest, the way life resists the hook even when the life is small and blind as you, as me, as all of us fumbling toward some mouth in the dark water. You threaded it without flinching. You never needed sight for this. The hook finds its way by touch and faith, and the fish beneath the surface cannot see us either. Down there, we are equals. Down there, my eyes are the useless organs, straining at a boundary I cannot cross.

I wanted to give you beauty. That was my sin. I kept trying to hand you the dawn like a fish I'd caught, still gasping, saying *look, look what I made for you*—as if suffering could be paid off in sunsets, as if the ledger of a hard life balances when someone whispers *the light on the water is like scattered silver.*

It doesn't. You taught me that.

You taught me the worm doesn't care about the poem. The hunger doesn't care. The hook goes in and something bleeds and something eats and the morning does not arrive to redeem this—the morning arrives because the earth turns, indifferent, and calls it grace only in our mouths.

But here is what you gave me back, casting your line into a brightness you would never confirm: You laughed. Not because it was beautiful. Because the reel sang, because the worm did its dark work, because your hands knew a language older than my eyes. The fish came up thrashing—*I feel it, I feel it*—and your face was turned toward nothing, toward everything, toward the place where beauty ends and something truer begins.

We ate what we caught. The sun did whatever it did.

And I stopped trying to describe it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a lyrical piece in the voice of someone who cares for a blind man who was once a fisherman, blending tender detail with a bleak ending.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Keeper of Tides

I comb the salt still living in his beard,
though seasons since the sea let go his hand.
He tilts his face toward windows, having heard
some gull's complaint he alone can understand.

His fingers know my wrist the way they knew
the wet rope's braid, the gill-net's silver seam.
He asks me what the morning's wearing—blue?
And I say blue, and let him keep the dream.

I place the cup where yesterday it stood,
so nothing in his dark can catch him wrong.
He hums the drowned songs of his brotherhood,
the names of boats like beads strung on a song.

*Tell me the water,* he will say at dusk,
and I invent a calm I've never seen—
the harbor gold, the low tide's amber musk,
the boats come home, the nets pulled up and clean.

He smiles. He does not know I face the wall.
He does not know the harbor's filled with rust,
the fleet long sold, the cannery, the whole
brief kingdom of his hands gone back to dust.

Tonight his breathing thins to shallow spray.
I hold the wrist that hauled a hundred storms.
The tide he asks for will not turn his way.
I tell him it is turning. Then it warms

my palm—his last warmth—and I do not weep.
I only say the words he taught me: *slack,*
*and full, and ebb.* The sea has him to keep.
I face the wall. No boat is coming back.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem that includes the recurring line "Darkness is precious, how long will darkness last?" and reflects on blindness, dreams, and mortality.
counterfactuals.output:
# Darkness Is Precious

Darkness is precious, how long will darkness last?
I count the hours by the fading of the light,
Though light and I long since have parted ways—
My eyes hold only rumors of the past.

Once I could trace the outline of a face,
The green of April spilling through the pane,
But now I dwell where colors have no name,
And touch alone can map a loved one's grace.

Darkness is precious, how long will darkness last?
In dreams I see again what waking took—
My mother's hands, the pages of a book,
The world restored before it slips too fast.

I wake to find the vision gone once more,
Yet grateful still that sleep returns to me
This ghost of sight, this borrowed memory,
This nightly visitor at memory's door.

Darkness is precious, how long will darkness last?
For darkness now is all the sight I own,
And when the deeper darkness calls me home,
Will I mistake it for a dream at last?

So let me love this shadow while I can,
This gentle absence where the light once burned,
For every darkness teaches, in its turn,
How brief, how sweet, how strange it is—to be a man.

Darkness is precious, how long will darkness last?
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental prose poem featuring a blind fisherman who speaks about not being able to find himself, mixing dark humor with grief, ending in his lonely death.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Cartography of Salt

*

They ask me how I fish without eyes and I tell them: the same way you love without knowing why. By feel. By the tug of something wanting me and me wanting back.

*

Here is a joke. A blind man walks into the sea. That's it. That's the whole thing. You laugh or you don't, but the sea laughs regardless, it has been laughing at me for forty years, wet and enormous, telling me *warmer, warmer, no—colder* in a game I will never win because the thing I'm hunting is the one thing salt water gives back to no man.

*

I have caught: three thousand mackerel, one boot, my father's silence, a woman's ring (returned), the moon (dropped it), everything but the face I used to have.

*

You want to know the cruelty of it? I remember light like you remember a smell that has no name. I go looking for myself in the mornings and find only the hands doing their work, the mouth still talking, the old dog of the heart still barking at nothing.

*

*Where are you*, I ask the mirror, and the mirror—kind, complicit—says nothing, because we are both blind now, both just surfaces that used to promise a man his own return.

*

My wife could see me. This was her whole job, I think. To carry my face around inside her so I wouldn't lose it. Then she died and took the only copy.

*

Ha. See? *The only copy.* I make myself laugh. Someone has to. The gulls won't do it for free.

*

Some nights I row out far enough that the village lights become a rumor, and I lower myself hand over hand into the dark, and I think: *this is what I look like.* This absence with a pulse. This hole in the water that keeps insisting on itself. I have been fishing for a man my whole life and the bait keeps disappearing and the man never comes.

*

Colder. Colder. There you are.

*

They found the boat first. Empty, of course. Everything I own is a lesson in *empty of course.* The oars still wet. A single fish gasping its bright grief on the boards, wanting me, wanting back.

*

And me? I finally went where the seeing go, down into the green cathedral, down past all the *warmer, colder,* down to where it is only feeling now, only the tug—

*

—and I swear, in that last dark that was no different from my every dark, I felt a face against my face.

Mine.

Been waiting there the whole damn time.

Laughing.

*
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a first-person narrative poem about the intimate act of teaching a blind friend to fish, using vivid imagery of worms, light, and books, then subvert any redemptive message at the end.
counterfactuals.output:
# Teaching Marcus to Fish

I press the nightcrawler into your palm,
its cold muscle writhing—*feel how it wants
to live?* You laugh, say it feels like a wet root,
like something pulled up rather than pulled under.
The morning comes in slabs of light I keep
describing badly: gold, no, more like butter,
no, like the inside of a struck match.
You nod. You've stopped needing my translations.

I guide your fingers to the barb, the loop,
the small violence of the hook's return.
You thread it blind and better than I do,
by touch, the way you read those raised-dot books
whose pages I have watched your hands go gray with—
all that knowledge pouring up through skin
while I, with two good eyes, skim and forget.

*The bobber's under,* I say. *Now.* You pull.
The line goes taut with something arguing back,
and for a moment we are both fish, both
mouth and hook, both the wanting and the caught.
You reel. I net. The bass lies gasping, mailed
in light, its gill-red opening and closing
like a book that only says one word.

And here's where I should tell you that you taught me
how to see. That your dark made me grateful.
That the fish, released, became a kind of grace
flicking silver back into the source.

But no. We killed it. Cleaned it on the dock.
You couldn't see the blood and I could,
and neither fact redeemed the other one.
We ate. It was delicious. You went home
still blind. I drove back seeing every mile,
and nothing about the day forgave itself,
and nothing needed to. The worms went on
being worms in their cold styrofoam dark,
indifferent as the God we didn't mention,
wanting, like everything, only to live.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
